local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 Michigan voters elect school board members in every school district, community college trustees, district library boards and the circuit, district and probate judges whose terms are up, all without party labels; villages and the cities whose charters put their elections in even years elect their officers; and vacancies on county boards and township boards are filled for the rest of a term, with a county executive in the counties that elect one this year. County clerks, treasurers, registers of deeds, prosecuting attorneys, sheriffs and drain commissioners, county commissioners and township boards were elected for four years in 2024 and are next elected in 2028, and most cities elect in November of odd-numbered years.
local_calendar.s: Michigan Election Law, MCL 168.642 and 168.642c (cities, villages and school boards), 168.200 and 168.358 (county and township officers), and MCL 46.410 (county commissioners); the Department of State's Official Candidate Listing (judges)

local_coverage.t: Loaded: the 163 circuit, district and probate court contests on the Department of State's Official Candidate Listing, each filed under the counties state law puts in its circuit or district; and the county clerks' own November lists for 12 of the 15 largest counties (Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Kent, Washtenaw, St. Clair, Jackson, Ottawa, Ingham, Kalamazoo, Saginaw and Muskegon): 630 contests (287 school board, 212 city and village, 88 township, 6 county, 37 college and library board) with 1725 candidates. Michigan has no statewide list of local candidates, so the other counties are not loaded yet and are named among the gaps. Left out everywhere: ballot questions, and candidates a list marks as withdrawn or disqualified. A school district that crosses a county line is shown for the counties whose lists print it, its home county and any county its official name states, and a college or a district library for the counties whose lists print it and any county a seat is named for; any of them may reach other counties. No ballot order is given: none of the lists states the order the ballot prints names in.

measures.t: A proposed initiated law to prohibit campaign contributions from certain regulated utilities and government contractors and apply campaign finance laws and regulations to additional types of political communications
measures.q:
The proposal would:
• Prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to these utilities/contractors from making direct or indirect campaign contributions to those who run for or hold offices that impact them.
• Expand laws regulating spending on political communications, including those requiring disclosing donor information, to apply to communications clearly identifying candidates or ballot questions, even if they do not expressly advocate voting for/against them.
• Expressly apply the law requiring disclosure of who paid for political communications to internet political communications.
Should this proposal be adopted?
measures.s: On November 3, 2026, Michigan electors will have the opportunity to vote on Proposal 2026-2, which would amend the Michigan Campaign Finance Act (MCFA) by amending Sections 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 44, 47, and 51, (MCLs 169.201, 169.203, 169.205, 169.206, 169.209, 169.244, 169.247, and 169.251) and adding Sections 30a and 30b. Proposal 2026-2 is the result of an initiative petition
measures.sb: The Senate Fiscal Agency, in its overview of the proposal. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: If a majority of the electors vote "yes" on Proposal 2026-2, the MCFA would be amended accordingly.
measures.f:
The proposal would have a minor negative fiscal impact on the Department of the Attorney General.
The proposal could have a minor negative fiscal impact on State district courts.
Adoption of the proposal would have negative and corresponding positive fiscal impacts on local government.
The proposal could have a negative fiscal impact on the Department of State, depending on the number of investigations into potential violations that it conducted.
measures.fb: The Senate Fiscal Agency, in its overview of the proposal: the opening sentence of each part of its fiscal section. It is not printed on the ballot.

measures.h: Placed on the ballot by an initiative petition for a law. The petition was filed by a ballot question committee, Michiganders for Money Out of Politics.

measures.t: Renewal of Wayne County Zoological Authority Millage in Support of the Detroit Zoo
measures.q:
In 2008 and 2016, pursuant to Public Act 49 of 2008, Wayne County voters renewed a 10-year property tax millage to fund zoological services through the Wayne County Zoological Authority, supporting animal care for more than 2,000 animals and 200 species, educational and senior programs, and facility maintenance at the Detroit Zoo.
To continue providing these services, the Authority seeks to renew and restore the millage to the original voter-approved rate of 0.10 mill (10 cents per $1,000 of taxable value). This proposal would renew the millage at 0.0982 mill and restore the remaining 0.0018 mill that was reduced due to required rollback, for a total authorized rate of 0.10 mill on taxable real and personal property for ten (10) years.
If approved, the millage rate would be unchanged from those approved by voters in 2008 and 2016. Funds will be disbursed to the Authority and transferred to the Detroit Zoo as permitted by law. All funds are subject to annual independent audits. It is estimated that $6,145,462 will be collected in the first year.
Ballot Question:
Do you approve the renewal and restoration of the levy of 0.10 mill on all taxable property in Wayne County for a period of ten (10) years, from 2028 through 2037?
measures.r: To pass, the millage needs more YES votes than NO votes among the voters who vote on it. (Michigan Constitution, article IX, section 31)
measures.nt: A proposal for every voter in Wayne County, in the words of the Wayne County Clerk's official list of proposals.

measures.t: Southeast Michigan Public Historical Museum Authority Millage Proposal
measures.q:
The Southeast Michigan Public Historical Museum Authority (“Authority”) is a joint authority established by Wayne and Oakland Counties (“Counties”) pursuant to Michigan Public Act 321 of the Public Acts of 2000, as amended, and was formed to support the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, Detroit Historical Museum, Dossin Great Lakes Museum, and other public historical museums located in Wayne and Oakland Counties (“Historical Museums”) that provide historical museum services for students, residents and visitors of the Counties. The law allows the Authority to seek authorization from the electors in each of the Counties to levy a tax of 0.2 mill (20 cents per $1,000 of taxable value) on taxable property to provide revenue for Historical Museums. It is estimated that if approved and levied on taxable property located within Wayne County, this new millage would generate approximately $12,219,200 in 2026.
In addition to supporting the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, Detroit Historical Museum, and Dossin Great Lakes Museum, 15% of revenues received by the Authority from taxable property in Wayne County, after Authority administrative expenses, will be disbursed to the County of Wayne for the purposes of supporting Historical Museums in Wayne County. Shall a 0.2 mill tax on all taxable property located within Wayne County be imposed by the Authority for a period of ten (10) years, being years 2026 through 2035, inclusive, to provide historical museum services for the benefit of the residents of the Counties?
measures.r: To pass, the millage needs more YES votes than NO votes among the voters who vote on it. (Michigan Constitution, article IX, section 31)

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Michigan Department of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the August 4 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, county offices are elected on party lines; school districts and other districts are nonpartisan; cities, villages and townships are some of each. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (August 4) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau, the Michigan Center for Educational Performance and Information, the Kalamazoo County Clerk/Register of Deeds, the Oakland County Clerk/Register of Deeds, the Saginaw County Clerk, the Washtenaw County Clerk/Register of Deeds, the Wayne County Clerk, the Kent County Clerk, the Jackson County Clerk, the Ingham County Clerk, the Macomb County Clerk / Register of Deeds, the Muskegon County Clerk and the St. Clair County Clerk, each named among these sources; where something on a county’s ballot could not be shown, that county’s page says what and why.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the Michigan Department of State, the State of Michigan and the Michigan Legislature: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For statewide offices, the Legislature, judges, county offices, mayors, city councils and school boards a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Candidates for township boards, soil and water, hospital and other small district boards and city clerks and treasurers show what they filed and, if they listed one, their campaign website. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: returns compiled precinct by precinct, close to but not the certified canvass (the sources say whose, and by how much they differ), added up here by county, city, village or township and district on the lines in force at that election. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are counted only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Published polls by other pollsters that we have checked against their own release are shown apart, under Other published polls, for reference, and are never counted in the average; the rest are counted and named. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from your precinct, where the map files place it, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: Sandbox: Reading & access, in lanes
items: A second sandbox experiment, on the draft site only: the reading and access settings sorted into six lanes (Language, How much, Text, Colour and contrast, Motion and calm, Ready-made sets). Open a lane and its settings are tabs: click one to pin it open, as many as you like, and your pins are kept on this device. Open another lane and it opens to the left of the first, so several can be open at once; on a phone they line up in a strip you swipe through.
The Language lane comes first and names every language with a finished translation in its own words. Choosing one shows the page again in that language, with the lane still open.
The settings are the site's own, so whatever is chosen there carries to every page. Every other page still opens the usual panel.

changelog.title: Final-week polls, Texas specials, Connecticut's towns, Election Night readiness
items: Final-week polls: 32 more polls, each checked against the pollster's own release. Polls by members of the Transparency Initiative count in the averages: Marquette, Marist, Siena, Michigan State, Concord, Emerson, Targoz, ActiVote and the University of North Florida, across Senate and governor races in Wisconsin, Maine, New York, Michigan, Nebraska, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Florida, and U.S. House districts NY-17, WA-03 and KY-06. Polls by others are shown apart and never averaged; those paid for by a campaign or a party say so. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena district polls, Emerson's subscriber-only district polls) are listed as waiting, not shown. The day's forecasts were made again with them.

Texas: the state's November 3 special elections for State House District 93 and State Senate District 22, the 276th District Court, a Democrat added to one judicial race, and nine declared write-ins are now on Texas's ballot pages, from the Secretary of State's own lists.

Connecticut: every town has now posted its sample ballot, and all are read: registrars of voters, town and school board contests, and every probate district now carry their candidates (110 local races, up from 76).

On state ballot pages, 43 kinds of local office that were listed at the end under their own titles (Florida's community development boards, library boards, receivers of taxes and others) now sit with the offices like them.

Election Night: Minnesota's saved results files are read about four times faster; Texas's two special elections and its judicial race are tied to the state's results; a new check holds back any state's file that shows votes before its polls close (three states' test files do today); and practice runs can no longer reach the public results.
Election Night counts 267 statewide races, and the U.S. page now names the District of Columbia's two offices apart from them. The Past results door now says all 50 states and DC are loaded.

State ballot pages: Georgia's and Virginia's mail-ballot notes no longer call October 23 "this Friday"; notes and source lines no longer describe how this site reads its files or show raw web addresses (each source's link is still there).

Wording: the news-outlet count now matches everywhere; the Method page says plainly that polls outside our average are shown apart; it says which Forecasts page lists every forecast; the privacy answers now name the Forecasts page's address look-up and street maps, and the Access page names the weather picture's one request; the page guide no longer says Minnesota is the only state with a forecast map.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

changelog.title: Every state on the forecast map
items: Each state on both Forecasts pages now has its map and "Your ballot, as forecast", with Share: all 40 states with a forecast, not Minnesota alone. Use your location or type your address, and the page lists every race on your ballot there with the model's forecast where it has one. Your location stays on your device.
A state's map and its list of races load only when you open that state.
In the states that drew new congressional lines for 2026, the map says so, and your U.S. House district is found only from the new lines, never the old ones.

The nine states with new U.S. House districts for 2026 (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah) now show those districts on the ballot maps, from the Census Bureau's 2026 plan files published October 6, and "Use my location" or a typed address finds your 2026 district there. Before, those maps showed only the state's outline.

A statewide board elected by district (Texas's State Board of Education and others) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is placed by its own district, or the page says it cannot tell which seat is yours.
Past results load from the site's own results store rather than from each copy of the site, which leaves more room for election week.

Where a state's precinct lines are not on file here, your ballot still lists its statewide races. A statewide board elected by district (a state board of education, a public service commission) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is counted among the races the page could not place, and the state's own ballot lookup is the authority.

x.es: Los fideicomisarios de un colegio comunitario dirigen un distrito de colegios comunitarios. Fijan sus reglas y los requisitos para graduarse, aprueban su presupuesto y eligen a su máximo líder.

council.t: The city or town council makes the city's laws. It also passes the budget and sets taxes and fees.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El concejo de la ciudad o del pueblo hace las leyes de la ciudad. También aprueba el presupuesto y fija los impuestos y las tarifas.

county_commissioner.t: The county's governing board passes the budget, sets taxes and oversees services like roads. Its members are called commissioners, and in some places supervisors or police jurors.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-11, Board of County Commissioners, North Dakota Legislative Branch
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: La junta de gobierno del condado aprueba el presupuesto, fija los impuestos y supervisa servicios como los caminos. Sus miembros se llaman comisionados y, en algunos lugares, supervisores o jurados de policía.

county_executive.t: This office runs the county's offices, while a separate elected council makes the laws. In Kentucky the county judge/executive also leads the county board.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives
Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: Este cargo dirige las oficinas del condado, mientras que un concejo elegido por separado hace las leyes. En Kentucky, el juez/ejecutivo del condado también dirige la junta del condado.

court_of_appeals.t: The court of appeals is the middle level of state courts. Its judges check trial court rulings for legal mistakes when one side appeals, and they do not hold new trials.
s: Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
How courts work, California Courts Self-Help Center
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice

x.es: El tribunal de apelaciones es el nivel intermedio de los tribunales del estado. Cuando una de las partes apela, sus jueces revisan si las decisiones de los tribunales de primera instancia tienen errores legales, y no celebran juicios nuevos.

district_court.t: In most of these states the district court is the main trial court, where most cases start. In Alabama, Michigan, Washington, New York and a few other states it is a lower court for minor crimes, traffic and small lawsuits.
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch
Jefferson County District Court (Alabama Code 12-12-30 and following), Alabama Unified Judicial System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Michigan Compiled Laws 600.8301 (district court jurisdiction), Michigan Legislature
North Carolina General Statutes 7A-272 (jurisdiction of district court), North Carolina General Assembly
Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Washington State Courts
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State

x.es: En la mayoría de estos estados, el tribunal de distrito es el principal tribunal de primera instancia, donde empiezan la mayoría de los casos. En Alabama, Michigan, Washington, Nueva York y algunos otros estados, es un tribunal inferior para delitos menores, casos de tránsito y demandas pequeñas.

governor.t: The governor is the state's top leader. The governor signs or vetoes new laws, names many state officials and leads the state's military forces.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article V (Executive Branch), Michigan Legislature

x.es: El gobernador es el líder principal del estado. El gobernador firma o veta las nuevas leyes, nombra a muchos funcionarios estatales y dirige las fuerzas militares del estado.

library_board.t: Library board members run a public library. They set its rules and yearly budget, care for its property and hire its director.
s: Michigan Compiled Laws 397.182, District Library Establishment Act, Michigan Legislature

x.es: Los miembros de la junta de la biblioteca dirigen una biblioteca pública. Fijan sus reglas y su presupuesto anual, cuidan sus bienes y contratan a su director.

mayor.t: The mayor is the city's elected leader and, in some cities, runs city departments. Where the council hires a city manager, the mayor leads the council and the manager does the daily work.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El alcalde es el líder elegido de la ciudad y, en algunas ciudades, dirige los departamentos municipales. Donde el concejo contrata a un administrador municipal, el alcalde dirige el concejo y el administrador hace el trabajo diario.

park_commissioner.t: A Michigan township park commission buys, runs and cares for the township's parks and beaches.
s: Michigan Compiled Laws 41.426 and 41.426a, Township Parks and Places of Recreation (Act 157 of 1905), Michigan Legislature

x.es: Una comisión de parques de un municipio de Michigan compra, administra y cuida los parques y las playas del municipio.

probate_court.t: A probate court handles wills and the estates of people who have died, and often guardianships. In New York the judge is the Surrogate, and the court also handles adoptions.
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State
Michigan Compiled Laws 700.1302 (probate court jurisdiction), Michigan Legislature
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch

x.es: Un tribunal de sucesiones se encarga de los testamentos y de los bienes de las personas fallecidas y, a menudo, de las tutelas. En Nueva York, el juez lleva el título de Surrogate, y el tribunal también se encarga de las adopciones.

school_board.t: The school board runs a public school district. It hires the superintendent, sets district rules, passes the budget and, in many states, sets the local school tax.
s: Statutory Requirements for School Districts, Informational Paper 29 (Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau), Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction
Board of Education, Mercer County Schools, Kentucky
SBDM Councils & School Board Duties, Oldham County Schools, Kentucky

x.es: La junta escolar dirige un distrito escolar público. Contrata al superintendente, fija las reglas del distrito, aprueba el presupuesto y, en muchos estados, fija el impuesto escolar local.

secretary_of_state.t: In most states, the secretary of state runs elections and keeps records, such as business filings. Other duties differ by state.
s: Secretary of State Divisions & Programs, Nebraska Secretary of State

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el secretario de estado administra las elecciones y guarda registros, como los documentos que presentan las empresas. Las demás funciones varían según el estado.

state_board_of_education.t: The state board of education sets rules for public schools across the state. These cover what students should learn, what they need to graduate, and in Texas, textbooks too.
s: SBOE Homepage, Texas State Board of Education
State Board, Kansas State Department of Education
Texas Education Code, Chapter 7 (State Board of Education powers and duties), Texas Legislature
Texas Education Code, Chapter 31 (instructional materials), Texas Legislature

x.es: La junta estatal de educación fija reglas para las escuelas públicas de todo el estado. Estas reglas abarcan lo que los estudiantes deben aprender, lo que necesitan para graduarse y, en Texas, también los libros de texto.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

x.es: La Cámara de Representantes del estado (llamada Asamblea o Cámara de Delegados en algunos estados) es la cámara más grande. Sus miembros redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

supreme_court.t: The state supreme court is the state's highest court. It hears appeals from lower courts and has the final say on state law (Texas also has a top court for criminal cases).
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Judicial System Structure, Supreme Court of Ohio

x.es: La corte suprema del estado es el tribunal más alto del estado. Atiende apelaciones de los tribunales inferiores y tiene la última palabra sobre la ley estatal (Texas también tiene un tribunal máximo para los casos penales).

town_clerk.t: The town clerk keeps the town's records and the notes of town meetings. In Michigan the clerk also runs elections, and in New York the clerk gives out some licenses.
s: Minnesota Statutes chapter 367, Town officers, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Local Government Handbook: Town Government, New York Department of State
Michigan Compiled Laws chapter 41, Townships, Michigan Legislature

x.es: El secretario del pueblo guarda los registros del pueblo y las actas de las reuniones del pueblo. En Michigan, el secretario también administra las elecciones y, en Nueva York, otorga algunas licencias.

town_supervisor.t: Town supervisors or trustees sit on the town board, which runs the town and its roads. In Michigan and New York the supervisor leads the board; Iowa trustees also run fire service and cemeteries.
s: Minnesota Statutes chapter 366, Town board, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Local Government Handbook: Town Government, New York Department of State
Michigan Compiled Laws chapter 41, Townships, Michigan Legislature
Township Governance in Iowa, Iowa Legislative Services Agency

x.es: Los supervisores o fideicomisarios del pueblo forman parte de la junta del pueblo, que administra el pueblo y sus caminos. En Michigan y Nueva York, el supervisor dirige la junta; en Iowa, los fideicomisarios también se encargan del servicio de bomberos y los cementerios.

town_treasurer.t: The town treasurer takes in the town's money, keeps a record of it and pays it out only when the town board says so.
s: Minnesota Statutes chapter 367, Town officers, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Michigan Compiled Laws chapter 41, Townships, Michigan Legislature

x.es: El tesorero del pueblo recibe el dinero del pueblo, lleva un registro de él y lo paga solo cuando la junta del pueblo lo indica.

university_board.t: These elected boards run a state university. They guide the school, control how it spends its money and choose its president.
s: Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article VIII, Section 5, Michigan Legislature
Laws of the Regents, Article 2: The Regents of the University of Colorado

x.es: Estas juntas elegidas dirigen una universidad estatal. Orientan a la institución, controlan cómo gasta su dinero y eligen a su presidente.

village_president.t: In a Michigan village the president is the top official. The president leads council meetings, votes on the council and sees that village laws are followed.
s: Michigan Compiled Laws 64.1, General Law Village Act (President), Michigan Legislature

x.es: En una villa de Michigan, el presidente es el funcionario principal. El presidente dirige las reuniones del concejo, vota en el concejo y vela por que se cumplan las leyes de la villa.
